To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the FasL expressed by activated T cells can mediate Fas-dependent cytolytic activity against Fas+ liver cells, leading to hepatocyte apoptosis.
Fas is an apoptotic signaling receptor that triggers cell suicide upon binding to its cognate ligand, FasL, which is expressed by activated lymphocytes.
FasL-expressing T cells induce apoptosis in Fas-exposing hepatocytes, resulting in liver injury.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the Fas/FasL system in liver damage in vivo.
the role played by the Fas-FasL pathway in the development of liver damage.
the mechanisms of cell death and the role of Fas in the development of autoimmune diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

lpr-mediated graft-vs.-host disease in lethally irradiated recipients reconstituated with MRL/lp lymphocytes is characterized by an intrahepatic accumulation of FasL+ T lymphocytes that can induce liver damage through a Fas-dependent apoptotic pathway.
the Fas/FasL pathway is involved in liver damage in this model of GVHD.
the Fas/FasL interaction between T cells and hepatocytes is a mechanism for the induction of apoptosis in the liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the liver damage observed in MRL/lpr chimeras is due to the interaction between donor-derived T lymphocytes bearing the FasL, which are activated by the graft-versus-host reaction, and Fas-exposing liver cells.
the lpr gene mutation in MRL/lpr strain mice leads to the overexpression of the Fas ligand (FASL) on T cells, which can mediate FAS-dependent cytotoxicity against normal Fas+ target cells.
FasL+ T lymphocytes infiltrating the liver can induce hepatocyte apoptosis via the Fas-FasL pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lpr-mediated graft versus host disease (GvHD) is a model to study the role of FasL in vivo.
the Fas-FasL pathway can be involved in a number of different liver diseases.
the lpr gene is a useful tool to study the role of the Fas pathway in liver injury.
